1) Verruca plana (flat warts) — Most likely. Rationale: onset in childhood, asymptomatic slowly spreading papules on dorsal hands with later forearm involvement fits HPV-induced plane warts which commonly present as multiple flesh‑colored, flat‑topped papules in children/young adults. Next step: focused skin exam (note flat‑topped, smooth surface), dermoscopy; if uncertain, punch biopsy ± HPV PCR.

2) Verruca vulgaris (common warts) — Possible. Rationale: warts on hands that began in childhood can be common warts (more keratotic/dome‑shaped) and may multiply over years. Next step: inspect for hyperkeratosis/black dots, dermoscopy; consider cryotherapy trial or biopsy if atypical.

3) Lichen nitidus — Less likely but plausible. Rationale: chronic, small, flesh‑colored to hypopigmented, asymptomatic papules favoring hands/forearms in children/young adults; lesions can persist for years. Next step: clinical exam for pinpoint, shiny, flat‑topped papules and biopsy if diagnosis unclear.

4) Keratosis pilaris (follicular papules) — Less likely. Rationale: common from childhood, symmetric follicular rough papules on extensor forearms/upper arms but dorsal hand predominance is atypical. Next step: check follicular distribution and rough/keratotic texture.

5) Granuloma annulare (papular/localized type) — Least likely. Rationale: can present as grouped papules on hands/forearms that slowly change, but typically form annular plaques and may have central clearing. Next step: look for annular configuration; biopsy can confirm.

Recommended immediate actions (to clarify diagnosis): focused dermatologic exam to document morphology (flat vs dome, umbilication, keratosis, follicular vs smooth), dermoscopy of lesions, and if uncertainty persists a punch biopsy with histology (and HPV testing if warts suspected).
